query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor percentage of hafnium (Hf) to the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will suppress the radiation‐induced Cr–V precipitation by altering the local chemical ordering and increasing lattice distortion, while maintaining negligible irradiation hardening and improving sinterability for bulk fabrication.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 (a quaternary refractory high‐entropy alloy) that, under energetic-particle irradiation to ~8 dpa at elevated temperatures, exhibits the formation of ~3–5 nm Cr–V rich precipitates with slight irradiation hardening.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor Hf addition (approximately 7–8 at%) into the alloy formulation to create a quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf alloy.
generation.conditions: Irradiation with energetic particles (e.g., 3-MeV heavy ions) to ~8 dpa at fusion-relevant temperatures around 1073 K, where precipitation is normally observed.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified short-range order (SRO) and increased lattice distortion due to Hf incorporation, which together suppress the nucleation and growth of Cr–V precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Hf addition is expected to alter the thermodynamic driving forces and kinetics of elemental segregation by increasing the overall mixing entropy and lattice distortion. This modification reduces the tendency for Cr and V to cluster under irradiation, while the improved sintering behavior of Hf-containing alloys promotes bulk consolidation without compromising the irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Hf-modified variant should exhibit a substantially lower density (or complete suppression) of Cr–V precipitates, retain nearly unchanged hardness under irradiation (i.e., negligible hardening), and offer improved bulk fabrication due to enhanced densification.
generation.baseline: The standard nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy that forms ~3–5 nm Cr–V rich precipitates (around 0.03 nm⁻² density) with a measured hardness of ~14 GPa and slight irradiation hardening after 8 dpa.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated under energetic-particle irradiation conditions up to 8 dpa and at temperatures near 1073 K; behavior outside these irradiation doses and thermal regimes may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While directional changes (precipitation suppression and non-increasing hardness) are expected, the precise quantitative reduction in precipitate density and the degree of improvement in sinterability require experimental validation and may depend on the exact Hf content and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the baseline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy and one of the modified quinary alloy with ~7–8 at% Hf. Subject both sets to energetic-particle irradiation (e.g., 3-MeV Cu+ ions) to an accumulated dose of ~8 dpa at ~1073 K. After irradiation, compare the microstructures and mechanical properties.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to assess the presence, size, and density of Cr–V precipitates.
Nanoindentation to measure hardness and detect any irradiation-induced hardening.
Evaluation of sinterability or bulk densification metrics during sample processing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified alloy shows a similar level of Cr–V precipitation (in terms of size and density) and comparable irradiation hardening to the unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11, or if its bulk fabrication properties do not improve, then the hypothesis that Hf addition suppresses radiation-induced precipitation while retaining negligible hardening and improving fabricateability is falsified.

The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
